newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FORECAST- HSBC sees Hong Kong growth slowing.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- HSBC sees Hong Kong growth slowing.

text.p: Hong Kong's economic growth is expected to slow down in the future because of its reliance on the service sector which looked set to expand more slowly, the Hong Kong and Shanghai Banking Corp Ltd said on Wednesday.
But its role as a financial hub for nearby China would help sustain the territory's economic expansion, the bank said in a research report.

"Over the past few years, Hong Kong's economic growth has slowed to around five percent per annum. Having attained a per capita income comparable with that of the industrialised nations, it is expected that Hong Kong's rate of expansion will slow to a pace similar to that of these countries," it said.
"It is generally accepted that the structural transformation towards a service-based economy has had a strong bearing on the territory's lower growth rate," it added.
Since the early 1980s, after China had opened its door to foreign investors, many Hong Kong manufacturers had been relocating their production to China where costs were lower.

"While the shift of human and capital resources from the manufacturing sector to be service sector (in Hong Kong) in the past few years has been a major force behind the rapid growth of the service sector, this momentum is unlikely to be sustained, as relocation of the manufacturing base to mainland China is near completion," the report said.
"Further expansion will therefore rely heavily upon increased productivity and capital investment," it added.
"The scope for improvement through capital investment in services, unlike manufacturing, is limited, however, due to the high labour content inherent in the sector," it said.
"Accordingly, Hong Kong's economy is expected to grow somewhat more slowly in the future," the report said.

The territory's gross domestic product is officially forecast to grow 4.7 percent in real terms in 1996, after growing 4.6 percent in 1995. The annual growth had averaged about seven percent over the past two decades.
While the service sector faced rising costs, there was limited feasibility for it to relocate operations to low-cost areas abroad in the way the manufacturing sector had done, the report said.
"The commitment of costs is essential in maintaining Hong Kong's external competitiveness," it said.

"Nevertheless, due to Hong Kong's role as a financial hub for China -- potentially the world's largest economy -- the ever-growing need for services will help to sustain the territory's economic expansion," it added.
